name: Hard-Easy Effect
description: Confidence can move in the wrong direction with task difficulty: on hard tasks people often overestimate how well they will do, while on easy tasks they can underestimate it. Difficulty distorts calibration, not just confidence level.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to self-assessment UX, education products, prediction interfaces, forecasting tools, AI-confidence displays, and internal planning rituals where teams must judge how well they or users will perform under easy vs. hard conditions.
myth_risk_note: Juslin, Winman & Olsson's (2000) quantitative review of two-alternative general-knowledge studies finds 'very little support for a cognitive-processing bias' underlying the hard-easy effect, arguing it largely disappears once scale-end effects and linear dependency are statistically controlled. Drugowitsch, Moreno-Bote & Pouget (2014) show hard-easy-effect-like miscalibration can arise from a rational mismatch between an observer's expected and the true task-difficulty distribution, rather than a genuine cognitive bias. This is a real, unresolved methodological dispute about whether the effect reflects true bias or a statistical/rational artifact -- not settled by the candidates available in this pass.
prevalence_note: Recognized in calibration, forecasting, and judgment-and-decision work, but the exact label is uncommon in mainstream product or UX discourse compared with broader 'overconfidence' language.

findings.description: Overconfidence is not a single unified phenomenon but reflects three distinct, dissociable effects: overestimation of one's own actual performance, overplacement of one's performance relative to others, and overprecision (excessive certainty in one's own judgments). Overestimation and overplacement reverse direction depending on task difficulty — people overestimate their absolute performance on hard tasks but underestimate it on easy tasks, while simultaneously believing they rank worse than others on hard tasks and better than others on easy tasks (the 'hard-easy effect'). Overprecision is more persistent across difficulty levels than the other two, and its presence reduces the apparent magnitude of both overestimation and overplacement.
